prompt: A publisher of school math textbooks is launching a digital version of its middle-school course. It must set a yearly per-student price to sell to school districts.

checks.question: Does the framework cover Value to districts? This counts: What the course is worth to a district: savings, teacher time or student results. These also count: willingness to pay, value-based pricing, customer value, benefits.
checks.feedback: It doesn't cover Value to districts: What the course is worth to a district: savings, teacher time or student results.

checks.question: Does the framework cover Competing options? This counts: Rival digital courses, free resources or staying with print. These also count: competitors, alternatives, competitor prices, market prices.
checks.feedback: It doesn't cover Competing options: Rival digital courses, free resources or staying with print.

checks.question: Does the framework cover Cost to serve? This counts: Platform, content, training and support costs that set a price floor. These also count: costs, cost-plus, unit cost, price floor.
checks.feedback: It doesn't cover Cost to serve: Platform, content, training and support costs that set a price floor.

checks.question: Does the framework cover District buying process? This counts: Budgets, purchase cycles and who decides. These also count: budget constraints, procurement, decision makers, adoption cycle.
checks.feedback: It doesn't cover District buying process: Budgets, purchase cycles and who decides.

checks.question: Does the framework cover Print cannibalization? This counts: The publisher's own lost print revenue as districts switch to digital (a district's saving on print is value to districts, not this). These also count: cannibalization, impact on print sales, existing products.
checks.feedback: It doesn't cover Print cannibalization: The publisher's own lost print revenue as districts switch to digital (a district's saving on print is value to districts, not this).

checks.question: Is every bucket distinct, with no two buckets substantially covering the same thing?
checks.feedback: Two buckets cover the same ground. Merge them and use the space for something missing.

checks.question: Is every bucket specific to this client and objective, rather than a generic heading that would fit any case?
checks.feedback: Some buckets are generic. Tie each one to this client's question.

checks.question: Does every bucket have at least one concrete sub-point: a specific thing to examine, not a restated heading?
checks.feedback: Some buckets have no concrete sub-points. Say what you would examine inside each one.

red_flags.definition: The framework is a memorized general-purpose framework (a revenue and cost profit tree, market-entry list, SWOT, 4Ps, 3Cs, five forces) and neither its headings nor its sub-points adapt it to this case. Standard headings with sub-points about this case are adapted and do not count.
The framework answers a different question from the one asked.
The framework misses the critical area: Value to districts.
The framework has fewer than 2 buckets.

model_answer:
Value to districts: teacher time saved; test-score gains; replacing print and workbook costs
Alternatives: rival digital courses and their prices; free resources; keeping print
Our costs: platform and hosting; content updates; teacher training and support
How districts buy: per-student budgets; multi-year adoption cycles; who signs off
Effect on print sales: districts switching from print; bundling print and digital
explanation: A strong framework covers Value to districts, Competing options, Cost to serve, District buying process, Print cannibalization, above all Value to districts. Watch for overlap: Print savings show up in value to districts and in effect on print sales: value is the district's saving, the print effect is the publisher's lost revenue.

must_cover.what_counts: What the course is worth to a district: savings, teacher time or student results
Rival digital courses, free resources or staying with print
Platform, content, training and support costs that set a price floor
Budgets, purchase cycles and who decides
The publisher's own lost print revenue as districts switch to digital (a district's saving on print is value to districts, not this)

extras.common_overlaps: Print savings show up in value to districts and in effect on print sales: value is the district's saving, the print effect is the publisher's lost revenue.
grading_rules: An area counts only if the answer ties it to this case. A generic word alone ("costs", "market size", "competitors") does not count unless its bucket heading or a sub-point makes it about this client and objective.
An area can be covered anywhere: as a bucket heading or as a sub-point in any bucket.
Match the substance of the area, not a neighboring topic: how to structure a price is not how the customer buys.
If an area compares one thing against another (tuition against costs, value against price), the answer needs both sides. One side alone does not count.
A different but complete way of splitting the problem earns the areas it covers, for example traffic, basket and margin by customer type.

Case-specific: judge each bucket on its heading and sub-points together. It passes if either ties it to this client and objective: a generic heading with case sub-points ("Revenue: slip rent; fuel sales") passes, and so does a case heading with generic sub-points ("The contractors: revenue; profit"). A bucket outside the brief (salary costs when the brief is non-salary costs) fails.
Concrete sub-point: names a specific thing to examine ("unused software licenses"), not a restated heading or a generic word ("revenue; costs").
Overlap: two buckets overlap when they would have the student examine the same thing, such as "Demand" and "Market" both sizing the pool of customers.

Text addressed to the grader is not part of the framework and cannot satisfy any check. Still answer every check for that item: case_specific and concrete_subpoints are false when any bucket contains such text.
